item.title: A private AI on a €1,900 card: what the Intel Arc Pro B70 changes for regulated professions
item.description:
On a €1,900 (ex-VAT) graphics card, a 27-billion-parameter model answers at more than 100 tokens per second, without any document leaving the company. What makes it possible: our port of the TensorFold engine to the Intel Arc Pro B70 card, now merged into the official project.

Replayable answers

an answer served alongside others equals the same answer served alone, on every try

The real obstacle is hosting

In an accounting firm, a notary’s office, a mutual insurer or an HR department, AI first runs into a simple question: where do the documents go? Client files, payslips or medical reports do not go to an external API, because professional secrecy and the GDPR forbid it.

item.title: TensorFold on Intel Arc Pro B70: from a Python port to a Zig engine
item.description: TensorFold only knew Macs and NVIDIA GPUs. We ported it to the Intel Arc Pro B70 card (Xe2 architecture, 32 GB), first in Python through PyTorch, then in Zig directly on Level Zero, with no PyTorch and no Python at run time. The second port has been part of the official project since TensorFold 1.0.12. This text gives the path, the pitfalls and the measurements, including the ones that are less favourable to us.

item.title: Serving Laguna S 2.1 NVFP4 on a single NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10): the complete runbook
item.description:
From the box killed by its own JIT compiler to a working 256K service. A 117.6B-parameter MoE (8.5B active), DFlash speculative decoding, native 256K context, all on a single unified-memory machine — no TP=2, no cross-node, no NCCL. Every command in this runbook is given verbatim.

Laguna fits on a single machine, where DeepSeek-V4 required two nodes and a coordination layer. The hard part is therefore no longer distribution but the box’s memory, which an unbridled JIT exhausts in a few seconds. This runbook covers the hardware context, the three traps that kill the boot, the complete single-node launch and the benchmark results measured on our hardware.

item.title: Running vLLM on an NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10): from git clone to NVFP4 inference
item.description:
The DGX Spark ships a GB10 GPU (Blackwell, SM121 compute architecture) on an aarch64 board. An architecture recent enough that several libraries of the CUDA ecosystem do not yet have a precompiled kernel for SM121. Three fixes that do not jump out of the official documentation, explained here from cloning the repository to launching an NVFP4-quantised model.

This article covers the full installation, from cloning the repository to the successful launch of an NVFP4-quantised model (Mistral-Small 119B), explaining why each step is necessary. All the commands are tested on our hardware; adapt the paths (~/models/..., model names) to yours.
